title: Helm & Kustomize
summary: Customise manifests with a kustomization file and kubectl -k; install, configure, upgrade and roll back packaged apps with Helm.

sections.heading: Kustomize in kubectl
sections.sourceTitle: Declarative Management of Kubernetes Objects Using Kustomize

blocks.text: Kustomize works from a sticker sheet (`kustomization.yaml`) layered over base forms. It can generate instruction sheets and sealed envelopes, stamp the same yard or tag on every form, and stack patches. Your radio (`kubectl`) reads them too. Preview with `kubectl kustomize <dir>`, then hand over the whole folder, not one file, with `kubectl apply -k`.
Kustomize customises Kubernetes objects through a **kustomization file** (`kustomization.yaml`). It is a standalone tool, and kubectl has also understood kustomization files since 1.14.

kubectl kustomize <kustomization_directory>   # render and print, nothing is applied
kubectl apply -k <kustomization_directory>     # -k is short for --kustomize

items: **Generate** resources from other sources (ConfigMaps and Secrets).
**Set cross-cutting fields** on every resource (namespace, name prefix/suffix, labels, annotations).
**Compose and customise** collections of resources (resources, patches, overlays).

blocks.text: Always preview with `kubectl kustomize <dir>` before `kubectl apply -k <dir>`. Note that `-k` takes a **directory** that contains a kustomization.yaml, not a file.

sections.heading: ConfigMap & Secret generators
sections.sourceTitle: Declarative Management of Kubernetes Objects Using Kustomize

blocks.text: Instead of writing instruction sheets and sealed envelopes by hand, a generator prints them from a file, an env list or literal lines. Each printout gets a fingerprint on its name (a content hash suffix), so new content means a new sheet. Your contract just names the sheet; Kustomize swaps in the fingerprinted name.

configMapGenerator:
- name: <cm-name>
  files:
  - application.properties   # whole file becomes one key
- name: <cm-name-2>
  envs:
  - .env                     # each line becomes its own key
- name: <cm-name-3>
  literals:
  - FOO=Bar
secretGenerator:
- name: <secret-name>
  literals:
  - username=<user>
  - password=<password>

items: Generated names get a **content hash suffix**, so changing the data produces a new ConfigMap or Secret.
Reference the generator's **name** in your Deployment; Kustomize rewrites it to the hashed name for you.
`generatorOptions` applies to all generators: `disableNameSuffixHash: true` turns the suffix off, and you can add shared `labels` and `annotations`.

sections.heading: Cross-cutting fields, patches & images
sections.sourceTitle: Declarative Management of Kubernetes Objects Using Kustomize

blocks.text: One sticker sheet can relabel every form at once: move them into a yard (`namespace`), add a `dev-` prefix, or add tags. Patches are small single-purpose stickers, applied in order; a JSON 6902 patch must name its target form. To swap a packing template, `images` changes its name or tag without any patch.

namespace: <namespace>
namePrefix: dev-
nameSuffix: "-001"
labels:
  - pairs:
      app: <app>
    includeSelectors: true
commonAnnotations:
  <key>: <value>
resources:
- deployment.yaml
- service.yaml
patches:
  - path: increase_replicas.yaml          # strategic merge patch
  - target:                               # JSON 6902 patch needs a target
      group: apps
      version: v1
      kind: Deployment
      name: <deployment-name>
    path: patch.yaml
images:
- name: nginx
  newName: <registry>/nginx
  newTag: "<tag>"

items: `resources` lists the files (or directories) to include.
`patches` supports **strategic merge** and **JSON 6902** patches, applied in the listed order. A JSON 6902 patch must name its `target`.
Keep patches small and single-purpose, for example one for replicas and one for memory limits.
`images` changes an image's name, tag or digest **without** writing a patch.
`replacements` copies a field from one resource (such as a prefixed Service name) into other resources.

sections.heading: Bases, overlays & -k commands
sections.sourceTitle: Declarative Management of Kubernetes Objects Using Kustomize

blocks.text: Keep one folder of master forms (the base). Each environment writes its own sticker sheet (an overlay) that points at the base and adds changes, like a `dev-` or `prod-` prefix. The base never knows who builds on it, so one base feeds many. With `-k`, your radio can apply, diff or delete it all.

A **base** is a directory with a kustomization.yaml and its resources. An **overlay** is a kustomization directory that lists other kustomization directories as its bases and customises them. A base never knows about its overlays, so one base can feed many.

# dev/kustomization.yaml
resources:
- ../base
namePrefix: dev-

# prod/kustomization.yaml
resources:
- ../base
namePrefix: prod-

kubectl apply -k <dir>/
kubectl get -k <dir>/
kubectl describe -k <dir>/
kubectl diff -k <dir>/      # compare with what applying would change
kubectl delete -k <dir>/

rows: Adds labels to all resources **and selectors**
Adds labels without automatically adding them to selectors
Prepends / appends to every resource name

blocks.text: Helm hands out pre-packed shipping kits (charts). Each delivery of a kit is a **release** with a name you choose. Helm 3 starts with no catalog, so add one with `helm repo add`. Fill in the forms with `-f` files (rightmost wins), and `--set` overrides those. Helm leaves the dock immediately unless you pass `--wait`.
Helm installs **charts** (packages). Each install creates a **release** with a name you choose. Helm 3 ships with **no default repository**, so you add one first.

helm repo add <name> <url>
helm repo update                 # refresh chart lists from repos
helm repo list
helm search repo <keyword>       # searches repos you added (local data)
helm search hub <keyword>        # searches Artifact Hub
helm show values <repo>/<chart>  # see configurable options
helm install <release> <repo>/<chart> -f values.yaml --set <key>=<value>
helm install <repo>/<chart> --generate-name
helm status <release>

items: `-f` / `--values` takes a YAML file and can be repeated; the **rightmost** file wins.
`--set` values are merged on top with **higher precedence** than `--values`.
`helm get values <release>` shows the values set on a release.
`helm install` can also install from a local `.tgz` archive, an unpacked chart directory or a full URL.
Helm does not wait for resources to be running before it exits (unless you pass `--wait`).

blocks.text: Every install, upgrade or rollback adds a page to the release logbook, starting at revision 1. Read `helm history` first, because `helm rollback` needs both the release and a revision number. Uninstalling throws the logbook away too, so there is nothing to roll back to unless you passed `--keep-history`.

helm upgrade -f <file>.yaml <release> <repo>/<chart>
helm history <release>             # list revisions
helm rollback <release> <revision>
helm uninstall <release>
helm list                          # releases Helm has kept a record of
helm list --deployed

items: Every install, upgrade or rollback adds **1** to the revision number. The first revision is always **1**.
`helm upgrade` only changes what differs from the last release. `--reset-values` clears earlier `--set` values.
`--wait` waits for Pods ready, PVCs bound and Services with an IP; `--timeout` defaults to `5m0s`. If the timeout is hit the release is marked FAILED.
`helm uninstall` removes the release record too, so you **cannot roll back** an uninstalled release. Use `--keep-history` to keep the record.

blocks.text: `helm rollback` needs both the release name and a revision number. Check `helm history <release>` first.

Open a kit box (a chart) and you find its label (`Chart.yaml`), default answers (`values.yaml`), fill-in templates, and any smaller kits it depends on. New form types in `crds/` go in first, and Helm never upgrades or removes them. A chart repository is simply a shop serving an `index.yaml` plus packed kits.

<chart>/
  Chart.yaml        # required: apiVersion, name, version
  values.yaml       # default configuration values
  charts/           # charts this chart depends on
  crds/             # CustomResourceDefinitions (plain YAML)
  templates/        # templates + values = manifests
  templates/NOTES.txt

items: Use `apiVersion: v2` for charts that need Helm 3 or later.
`version` is the chart's SemVer version; `appVersion` is the app's version and is only informational.
The defaults file inside a chart must be called `values.yaml`; files on the command line can have any name.
Templates read values from `.Values` and predefined values such as `Release.Name` and `Release.Namespace`.
CRDs in `crds/` are installed before the templates, are **never** upgraded or deleted by Helm, and cannot be templated.
`helm create <name>` scaffolds a chart, `helm lint` checks it and `helm package` builds the `.tgz`.

blocks.text: A chart **repository** is an HTTP server that serves an `index.yaml` plus packaged charts.

`helm template` fills in a kit's forms at your own desk and prints them, without ever radioing the front desk. It is a dry run on paper only: nobody at the office checks the forms, so a clean printout does not prove the port will accept them, for example that an API is supported.
`helm template` renders a chart's templates **locally** and prints the manifests. It doesn't contact the cluster: in-cluster lookups are faked and no server-side validity checks run.

helm template [NAME] [CHART] [flags]
helm template <release> <chart> -f <values>.yaml --set <key>=<value> -n <namespace>
helm template <release> <chart> --output-dir <dir>   # write files instead of stdout
helm template <release> <chart> -s templates/<file>.yaml   # --show-only one template
Because no server-side checks run, a clean render does not prove the cluster will accept the manifests (for example, that an API is supported).

flashcards.front: Render a kustomization directory without applying it?
Why does a generated ConfigMap have a suffix like -8mbdf7882g?
flashcards.back: Kustomize appends a content hash so new data creates a new object. Turn it off with generatorOptions.disableNameSuffixHash: true.
files embeds a whole file as one key; envs turns each line of the .env file into its own key.
commonLabels also adds the labels to selectors; labels adds them without automatically injecting selectors.
A base is a kustomization dir with resources; an overlay is a kustomization dir that references bases and customises them. Bases don't know about overlays.

flashcards.front: What does a JSON 6902 patch in kustomization.yaml require?
flashcards.back: A target (group, version, kind, name) so Kustomize knows which resource to patch.

flashcards.front: Add a Helm chart repository and refresh it?
flashcards.back: helm repo add <name> <url> then helm repo update.
--set wins over --values/-f. With several -f files, the rightmost wins.
helm rollback <release> <revision>. Find revisions with helm history <release>.

flashcards.front: Revision number after install, then upgrade, then rollback?
Keep the release record when uninstalling?
Which file in a chart is required?
Does Helm upgrade or delete CRDs from a chart's crds/ directory?
flashcards.back: No. Helm only creates them on install; it never reinstalls, upgrades or deletes them.

questions.stem: Which command applies the resources defined by the kustomization.yaml in the current directory?

options.explanation: -k (--kustomize) points kubectl at a kustomization directory.
-f applies manifest files; it does not run the kustomization.
This only renders and prints the output; it doesn't apply it.
That views the objects; it doesn't apply them.

questions.stem: You change a literal in a `configMapGenerator` and re-apply. What happens to the ConfigMap name?

options.text: A new ConfigMap with a different hash suffix is generated, and references are updated to it
options.explanation: The content hash suffix changes when the content changes.

options.text: The existing ConfigMap is edited in place with the same name
options.explanation: Only when disableNameSuffixHash is true does the name stay fixed.

options.text: Kustomize refuses to apply because the name is taken
options.explanation: The hash suffix avoids that clash.

options.text: The Deployment keeps pointing to the old name
options.explanation: Kustomize rewrites references to the generated name.

questions.stem: Which kustomization field stops the hash suffix on generated ConfigMaps and Secrets?

options.explanation: generatorOptions modifies all ConfigMap and Secret generators.
nameSuffix appends text to all resource names; it doesn't control the hash.
That adds annotations to all resources.
That copies field values between resources.

questions.stem: Which are cross-cutting fields you can set in kustomization.yaml for all resources? Select 3.

options.explanation: Sets the same namespace on all resources.
Prepended to every resource name.
Adds annotations to all resources.
That generates ConfigMaps; it doesn't set a field across all resources.

questions.stem: You want to replace `spec.replicas` with a JSON 6902 patch file `patch.yaml`. What else must the `patches` entry contain?

options.text: A target naming group, version, kind and name of the resource
options.explanation: Specifying target is mandatory for a Json6902 patch.
images changes image names/tags, unrelated to JSON patches.
Generators create ConfigMaps/Secrets.

options.text: Nothing, Kustomize finds the resource from the patch body
options.explanation: That's how strategic merge patches are matched, not JSON 6902 ones.

questions.stem: A dev overlay should reuse the manifests in `../base` and prefix all names with `dev-`. Which kustomization.yaml does that?

options.explanation: Overlays reference bases via resources and add cross-cutting fields.
A base has no knowledge of its overlays.
Without resources, nothing is included; and a suffix is appended, not prepended.
That field takes strategic merge patch files, not a base directory.

questions.stem: True or false: `kubectl diff -k <dir>` shows how the cluster would change if the kustomization were applied.

options.explanation: Correct: diff -k compares live objects with the rendered kustomization.
It does exactly that comparison.

questions.stem: A fresh Helm 3 install has no repositories. Which command adds one named `<name>`?

options.explanation: Helm 3 ships without a default repo; add one with helm repo add.
update refreshes repos that are already added.
That searches Artifact Hub; it doesn't add a repo.
install creates a release from a chart.

questions.stem: You run `helm install <rel> <chart> -f a.yaml -f b.yaml --set replicaCount=3`. Both files also set replicaCount. Which value is used?

options.explanation: --set is merged into --values with higher precedence.
The rightmost file wins among -f files, and --set beats both.
b.yaml beats a.yaml, but --set has higher precedence still.
Defaults are overridden by user-supplied values.

questions.stem: An upgrade broke release `web`. `helm history web` shows revisions 1–3. How do you return to revision 2?

options.explanation: helm rollback [RELEASE] [REVISION].
That upgrades again and clears --set values; it doesn't restore revision 2.
That removes the release from the cluster.
That only shows the release's values.

questions.stem: Which statements about Helm revisions and uninstall are correct? Select 2.

options.text: The first revision of a release is always 1
options.explanation: Stated in the Using Helm guide.

options.text: A rollback also increments the revision number
options.explanation: Install, upgrade and rollback each add 1.

options.text: You can roll back a release after a plain helm uninstall
options.explanation: Uninstall deletes the release record, so rollback is no longer possible.

options.text: helm uninstall keeps the release record by default
options.explanation: You need --keep-history for that.

questions.stem: What does `--wait` do on `helm install` or `helm upgrade`?

options.text: Waits until Pods are ready, PVCs bound and Services have an IP, up to --timeout
options.explanation: Otherwise Helm exits without waiting for resources.

options.text: Waits 5 minutes before starting the install
options.explanation: 5m0s is the default --timeout, not a delay.
That's --no-hooks.
That's helm template.

questions.stem: True or false: When you upgrade a release, Helm also upgrades the CRDs in the chart's `crds/` directory.

options.explanation: Helm never installs CRDs on upgrade or rollback, and never reinstalls existing ones.
Correct: CRDs are only created on install; upgrade or delete them manually.

questions.stem: Which file must every Helm chart contain?

options.explanation: Chart.yaml is required and holds apiVersion, name and version.
Optional.
Optional usage notes.
Optional plain-text licence file.

questions.stem: Which statement about `helm template` is correct?

options.text: It renders chart templates locally and prints the manifests
options.explanation: That's its synopsis.

options.text: It checks against the cluster that every API used is supported
options.explanation: No server-side validity testing is done.

options.text: It installs the release first, then prints the manifests
options.explanation: It only renders locally.
--output-dir is optional and writes files instead of stdout.
